check-reading-in-a-type-signature.title: Check: reading -> in a type signature

questions.question: isVowel :: Char -> Bool. Read strictly left to right, what does this say?
options: isVowel takes a Bool and gives back a Char
isVowel takes a Char and gives back a Bool
isVowel takes nothing and gives back a Char and a Bool
isVowel is a Bool that happens to be named Char
questions.explanation: Applying the gloss 'takes a(n) A, and gives back a(n) B' to Char -> Bool gives exactly this: isVowel takes a Char, and gives back a Bool.
optionFeedback: This reverses the arrow. The type to the left of -> is what is taken in; the type to the right is what comes back.
Correct. Left of the arrow is the input type, right of the arrow is the output type — read strictly in that order.
A single -> always separates exactly one input description from one output description at that stage; it is not a list of two unrelated types.
-> is not part of either type here; it is the separator between the input type and the output type.

questions.question: describe :: Int -> Int -> String -> String has three arrows. Reading one arrow at a time, what does describe take and give back overall?
options: It takes one String and gives back three values
It takes an Int, an Int, and a String, and gives back a String
It takes a String and gives back an Int
It cannot be determined without knowing describe's implementation
questions.explanation: Reading left to right, one arrow at a time: takes an Int, gives back [takes an Int, gives back [takes a String, gives back a String]]. Chained into an everyday reading, that is exactly: takes an Int, an Int, and a String, and gives back a String.
optionFeedback: This has the direction backwards — String only appears as an input in the third position and as the final output, not as the sole input.
Correct. Three arrows, three inputs consumed in order (Int, Int, String), with a String coming back at the end.
This reads the signature back to front; the first two positions are Int, not the last one.
A type signature alone is exactly what determines this reading — no implementation is needed, only the arrows and the types between them.

questions.question: A lab asks you to compute 30 factorial. Which type is the safer choice, and why?
options: Int, because it is the default numeric type
Integer, because it grows as needed and will not silently overflow a bounded maximum
Double, because factorials are always large numbers
Bool, because the result is either correct or incorrect
questions.explanation: 30 factorial is a huge whole number, far beyond what a fixed-width Int can represent safely on many systems. Integer has no upper bound (beyond available memory), which is exactly the property factorialResult relies on in this lesson's example.
optionFeedback: Int is bounded — it has a maximum and minimum value — which is precisely the risk this section warns about for large whole-number results.
Correct. Integer is arbitrary-precision, so it keeps growing as needed instead of wrapping around or overflowing.
A factorial is a whole number, not a value with a fractional part; using Double would introduce needless approximation for a calculation that should be exact.
The factorial itself is a number, not a true/false answer — Bool has no meaningful role here.

questions.question: Which of these is rejected by Haskell's type checker, and why?
options: (1, 'a', True)
[1, 'a', True]
questions.explanation: A list requires every element to share one type. [1, 'a', True] mixes a number, a Char, and a Bool — three different types — inside square brackets, which a list cannot represent.
optionFeedback: [1, 2, 3] is a perfectly ordinary list of numbers — every element shares one type.
A tuple's whole design is to hold different types at different fixed positions, so (1, 'a', True) is exactly what tuples are for.
Correct. Lists require one shared element type; mixing Integer, Char, and Bool inside [ ] is exactly the invalid case this section describes.
['a', 'b', 'c'] is a list of three Char values — one shared type throughout, so it is valid.

questions.question: (String, Integer) and (Integer, String) are described as different types. Why does position matter for tuples but not for lists?
options: It does not actually matter; the two tuple types are secretly identical

A tuple's type records the type at each fixed position, so swapping positions changes which type appears where; a list only records one shared element type, so element order does not affect the type itself
Lists cannot have more than one element, so order is meaningless for them
Tuples are always sorted automatically by type
questions.explanation: A tuple type is literally a sequence of per-position types. (String, Integer) means 'a String first, then an Integer'; reversing the positions describes a different shape entirely. A list's type is just [ElementType] regardless of how many elements it holds or their order.
optionFeedback: The lesson states this directly: '(String, Integer) and (Integer, String) are different types' — they are genuinely distinct, not merely differently written.
Correct. This is exactly the structural difference between the two: fixed per-position types versus one shared element type.
Lists can hold any number of elements, including many; order among those elements has no bearing on this point.
Nothing about tuples involves automatic sorting; a tuple's positions are fixed by where each value was written, not reordered by type.

questions.question: Applying the mechanical method to not (3 < 5), why is step 3 — '3 < 5 :: Bool' — established before step 6 works out the actual True/False answer?
options: Because arithmetic must always be calculated before any type is known

Because the method's first question is always 'is it well typed?' — not requires a Bool argument, so confirming that 3 < 5 produces a Bool is what licenses passing it to not at all, before the specific answer is worked out
Because 3 and 5 are not really compatible numeric values
The step order in the method does not matter; it is just a stylistic presentation choice
questions.explanation: The lesson's two questions are asked in a fixed order: 'Is it well typed?' before 'what value does it produce?' Establishing 3 < 5 :: Bool confirms not can legally accept it — not :: Bool -> Bool — before the method moves on to actually evaluating the comparison.
optionFeedback: This gets it backwards for this method: type-checking happens before evaluation, not the other way around, and a type error stops the process before any arithmetic runs.
Correct — this is exactly the two-question method: confirm well-typedness first, using the pieces' types, and only then work out the concrete value.
3 and 5 are both ordinary numeric literals and compare compatibly; that is exactly why 3 < 5 :: Bool holds in step 3.
The lesson presents 'Is it well typed?' as the first question specifically because a type error stops everything else — not 3 is rejected at that first question, before any evaluation is attempted.

questions.question: :type (7 + 1) reports 7 + 1 :: Num a => a, yet typing 7 + 1 at the ghci> prompt shows 8 with no ambiguity error. Why the difference?
options: :type and direct evaluation always disagree; this is a known inconsistency
:type reports the general, not-yet-defaulted type; evaluating the expression forces GHCi to display a concrete value, which triggers the defaulting rule and picks Integer
7 + 1 is secretly a different expression from (7 + 1)
GHCi always assumes Int, never Integer, for any bare numeric literal
questions.explanation: Asking for a type with :type does not require producing a concrete value, so GHC leaves the constraint general. Actually evaluating the expression requires showing a result, which forces a concrete choice — Haskell's defaulting rule supplies Integer for an unconstrained Num.
optionFeedback: They are not inconsistent — they are answering two different questions: 'what is the general type' versus 'what concrete value comes out when I actually run this'.
Correct. :type reports the general type before defaulting is needed; evaluating forces a concrete type via the defaulting rule, landing on Integer.
Parentheses around an already-complete expression change nothing about its meaning or its type here.
The lesson's own transcript shows it :: Integer after evaluating an ambiguous Num expression, not Int.

questions.question: Why does 2.5 default to Double instead of Integer?
options: Double is simply GHC's default type for every expression
2.5 requires the Fractional class because of its decimal point, and Integer does not belong to Fractional, so the defaulting rule moves on to Double, which does
GHC picks randomly between Integer and Double whenever a decimal point is present
2.5 is not actually a valid Haskell expression
questions.explanation: A literal with a decimal point needs Fractional, a class Integer does not belong to (Integer is whole numbers only). Since Integer cannot satisfy the constraint, the defaulting rule tries the next candidate, Double, which is Fractional.
optionFeedback: Integer, not Double, is the rule's first choice generally — Double is only reached because Integer fails to satisfy Fractional in this specific case.
Correct. This is exactly the reasoning that separates 2 + 3 (defaults to Integer) from 2.5 (defaults to Double): which typeclass is actually required.
The choice is not random; it follows the same deterministic defaulting rule every time, based on which typeclass constraint remains.
2.5 is an ordinary, valid floating-point literal — it evaluates and displays without any error.

check-static-types-versus-lazy-values.title: Check: static types versus lazy values

questions.question: Why is 'Haskell is lazily typed' inaccurate?
options: Because Haskell has no type system
Because Haskell is statically typed; laziness describes when well-typed values are evaluated, while type inference still happens before execution
Because every Haskell expression is evaluated immediately
Because lazy evaluation applies only to Strings
questions.explanation: Static typing and lazy evaluation answer different questions. GHC checks whether expressions fit their types before running the program; only the calculation of a valid expression's value may be postponed until demanded.
optionFeedback: Haskell has a strong static type system; the confusion is between typing and evaluation, not an absence of types.
Correct. Inference may spare you from writing a signature, but it does not postpone checking until run time.
That describes strict evaluation, the opposite of Haskell's normal non-strict strategy.
Laziness applies broadly to expressions and data structures, not only text.

deeper-reasoning-types-inference-and-rea.title: Deeper reasoning: types, inference, and reading errors

questions.question: GHC rejects the definition below, reporting that it expected Double but found Integer at the argument a. A student protests: "The signature says the result is a Double, so Haskell should convert the answer for me." Which diagnosis and repair is the most complete?
options: Haskell would convert the result automatically, but only if the module imports Data.Ratio; the error is a missing import rather than a type problem.

The / operator needs both of its operands and its result to be the same fractional type. The signature makes the result a Double, so (a + b) must also be a Double, but a and b are Integer values. A conversion such as fromIntegral (a + b) / 2 fixes it, as would taking Double arguments.
Replace / with div. div always returns a Double, so the signature will then be satisfied without any conversion.
The literal 2 is an Integer and is the only conflicting piece; writing 2.0 instead of 2 repairs the definition.
questions.explanation: A signature is a contract about the whole expression, and it also constrains the pieces inside it. Because / produces a Double here, its operands must be Double too. Haskell never silently converts between Integer and Double; fromIntegral is the explicit conversion. Changing the argument types in the signature is the other honest repair.
optionFeedback: No import changes how Haskell treats Integer and Double. Haskell does not insert numeric conversions automatically, so the fix has to appear in the code.
Correct. The error is blamed on a, the first operand that cannot be a Double, and the repair either converts it explicitly or changes the declared types.
div is for whole-number division and returns an integral type, not a Double. Using it here would produce a different type error, and 7 `div` 2 would also discard the fractional part.
The literal 2 is not the problem: a numeric literal such as 2 can already be read as a Double. The conflict is with a and b, which the signature fixes as Integer.

questions.question: A classmate says the script below cannot work: "Haskell is statically typed, so every function must declare its type, and main must be written as main :: IO ()." A second classmate says: "GHC just guesses the types and hopes for the best." Which statement best describes what actually happens, and what is given up by leaving signatures out?
options: The first classmate is right, and GHC refuses to load the file because the signatures are missing.
The second classmate is right: GHC defaults every unannotated function to Int and checks nothing else.

GHC infers each type from how the definition uses its values: double is Num a => a -> a, isLarge is (Ord a, Num a) => a -> Bool, and main is IO (). This is deduction from constraints, not guessing. What is lost by omitting signatures is a written contract, so a mistake is reported where it is used rather than where it was made.
Types are not checked at all in a file without signatures; they are checked while the program runs, as in a dynamically typed language.
questions.explanation: Type inference collects constraints from the operators and functions used in each body and picks the most general type that satisfies them. The file is fully type checked before it runs. Signatures remain good practice because they document intent and move errors closer to their cause, which is why this course asks for them.
optionFeedback: Signatures are optional. The file loads and runs, and GHC reports the same types that you could have written yourself.
There is no default of Int for functions. GHC infers the most general type that fits, which here is a type class constraint rather than any single concrete type.
Correct. Inference is a systematic deduction, and the cost of dropping signatures is clarity and error locality, not safety.
Haskell checks types before the program runs, whether or not signatures are written. A type error prevents evaluation entirely.

questions.question: A student expects both print lines below to show the same number, "because the brackets only add decoration." Which evaluation of the program is correct, and what rule explains it?
options: Both lines print 49, because Haskell always evaluates the whole line before applying a function.
The first line is a type error, because + cannot be used on the result of a function without brackets.
Both lines print 13, because brackets are ignored by Haskell when they surround numbers.

The first line prints 13 and the second prints 49. Function application binds more tightly than any operator, so square 3 + 4 is (square 3) + 4 = 9 + 4, while the brackets in the second line force 3 + 4 to be computed first, giving square 7 = 49.
questions.explanation: Function application, written with a space, has the highest precedence. Brackets are the tool for overriding it: they change which subexpression becomes the argument. They are never decoration in Haskell.
optionFeedback: Haskell does not evaluate a whole line first. Application binds to the nearest argument, so square takes only 3 in the first line.
square 3 produces an Integer, and + accepts Integers, so the first line is well typed. The only question is what square receives.
Brackets change meaning. Without them square receives 3 only; with them it receives 7.
Correct. The two lines differ exactly where the brackets change the argument to square.

questions.question: GHC prints the message below when this file is loaded. A student says: "It says Integer and [Char], so the whole line is wrong and I should rewrite the function from scratch." Which reading of the message is the most useful, and what repair question should follow?
options: The message points at a specific place: line 3, column 19, the argument "5" in the second position of (+). It needs an Integer there but found text. The repair question is what "5" should have been, which is almost certainly the number 5 rather than the string.
The message means that + cannot be used inside a function that has a signature, so the signature should be deleted.
The message means n is the wrong type, so the type of n should be changed to String in the signature, which makes the + legal.
The message is too general to act on; the only reliable approach is to try random changes until the file loads.
questions.explanation: GHC's message names the file, line and column, then the two types in conflict, then the smallest expression involved. Reading it from the top down narrows the search to one subexpression. GHC diagnoses; the programmer decides which side of the conflict was the mistake.
optionFeedback: Correct. The location, the expected and actual types, and the named argument together isolate the fault to a single token.
The signature is not the problem and + works perfectly well in functions with signatures. Deleting the signature would only change where a mistake is reported.
Changing the signature to accept a String would make + fail even more, since strings do not support +. The conflict is about the literal, not about n.
The message is precise. Random edits ignore all the information it provides.
